rendered: The authors did not run the Cyrene separation itself at room temperature. Their process is designed for elevated temperature, because PVDF binder is barely soluble in Cyrene at low temperature. The room-temperature runs were a comparison: the authors filtered at room temperature and at high temperature, and compared the results (see Fig. 3[1]). The stated reason for the comparison is that PVDF re-precipitates when the mixture cools: PVDF would precipitate out if the temperature was low[2]. The room-temperature filtered powder showed PVDF's signature band, which the authors read as evidence of the reprecipitation of PVDF along with the cathode particles after[3] cooling. The hot-filtered powder lacked that band, showing the binder had been removed. So the room-temperature run served as a control that shows why the separation must be kept hot, and the hot filtration is the step that avoids re-precipitation. This is consistent with the solubility data, in which the binder was the PVDF binder was barely soluble in Cyrene[4] 80 °C[5] and dissolved only at higher temperature.
